subject: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?

messages.author: 92a46c9449c605e2
messages.subject: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?
parts:
Hi,

I'm trying to figure out how to create a summary of data that includes
a column for indicating the row's percentage of the total statistic
(i.e. all data) and of its parent category's total.

I've read "The split-apply-combine strategy for data analysis" but
still can't quite figure out how to do this efficiently. I'm trying
to overcome the shortcoming of Excel's pivot tables, which do not
allow for calculating % of categories.

For example (using the 'baseball' data set) ... Given all data for
2007 where the number of home runs is greater than zero, summarize the
data using the following columns: League, Player ID, # of HRs, % of
Total HRs, % of League's Total HRs.

The following code creates the first three columns ... but not sure
where to go from there.

myfun <- function(x) sum(x$hr)
baseball <- subset(baseball, year == 2007 & hr > 0)
df2007 <- ddply(baseball, .(lg, id), myfun)
names(df2007)[3] <- "HR"

Might anyone have any recommendations?

Many thanks,
Mauricio

messages.author: 0c39e60ddb38622b
messages.subject: Re: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?
parts:
Hi:

Here is a two stage approach: one for the league percentages and one
for the overall MLB percentages. The key in ddply() is that an
external function passed into it needs to take a data frame as input,
and output a scalar or data frame; in this case, you want the latter.

myfun <- function(df) {
hrpct <- with(df, round(100 * hr/sum(hr), 3)
data.frame(id = df$id, hr = df$hr, pctlg = hrpct)
}

bb07 <- subset(baseball, year == 2007 & hr > 0)
bb07lg <- ddply(bb07, .(lg), myfun) # returns percentages of league HRs
ddply(bb07lg, .(), transform, pctmlb = round(100 * hr/sum(hr), 3))[, -1]

The [, -1] part at the end of the last statement removes a column of
unnecessary NAs.

HTH,
Dennis

messages.author: 3a775dfa0a96bf95
messages.subject: Re: Summarizing % of total and % of category ?
parts:
To my mind, the "natural" way to solve this is with nested ddply's, since the problem statement is also nested.

e.g.

ddply(baseball,
      .(),
      function(all) {
         total <- sum(all$hr)
ddply(all,
      .(lg),
      function(league) {
         lg_total <- sum(league$hr)
 ddply(league,
       .(id),
summarize,
HR=sum(hr),
HRlg=sum(hr)/lg_total,
HRtot=sum(hr)/total
)})})

Unfortunately, there is a bug in the handling of variable scope in ddply, so this won't work.  Instead, you have to use <<- (!):

ddply(baseball,
      .(),
      function(all) {
         total <<- sum(all$hr)
ddply(all,
      .(lg),
      function(league) {
         lg_total <<- sum(league$hr)
 ddply(league,
       .(id),
summarize,
HR=sum(hr),
HRlg=sum(hr)/lg_total,
HRtot=sum(hr)/total
)})})

A disadvantage of this approach is that you can't take advantage of the implicit scope rules of ddply, where a column name standing on its own refers to the column of the current data frame, thus you need to write, e.g. league$hr instead of hr.

There is another bug that introduces the meaningless .id column in the result....

           -s
